questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Play text and what performance adds
questions.learningObjective: Identify what performance adds to a printed play.
questions.stem: In a city planner's memo, a play's published text is compared with a live performance where the actors pause before a key line. What does the performance add?

options.text: It adds the sense of what the characters look like to each other
options.misconception: believes performance is mainly about physical appearance

options.text: It adds new events that never appear in the printed version
options.misconception: assumes performance invents material absent from the text

options.text: It adds timing and pace that the printed dialogue cannot record
It adds the exact words the playwright intended but cut for length
options.misconception: imagines performance recovering a lost original text

questions.explanation: Performance supplies what print leaves out, and pauses before a line are timing a reader cannot see. Appearance, new events and recovered drafts describe things the text alone cannot explain.
questions.hint: Ask what the page cannot show about a line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how delivery changes a character's presence.
questions.stem: A planner's memo notes that a character speaks mostly in replies to others in the published version but delivers long set speeches in performance. What does the memo make of that shift?

answer.exemplar: The memo treats the shift as evidence that performance changes the shape of a character's presence. Lines that read as responses on the page become sustained statements onstage, so the character's weight in the story rises without a single word being altered, which shows how much of character lives in delivery rather than in text.

questions.explanation: The same lines behave differently once they are spoken at length, so delivery alters a character's presence without changing the words. The memo is describing what the text leaves open.
questions.hint: Ask what changes when replies become speeches.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a soliloquy asks an audience to do.
questions.stem: A memo defends a character's soliloquy by arguing that it simply reveals what the character is thinking. Which reply holds up?

options.text: The reply holds because soliloquies exist to state a character's thoughts
options.misconception: accepts the convention without questioning its effect

options.text: The reply holds because a soliloquy asks the audience to judge what it reports
The reply holds because a soliloquy is the only private speech on stage
options.misconception: grounds the case in the technical fact of privacy alone

options.text: The reply holds because audiences prefer hearing plans stated plainly
options.misconception: argues from audience preference rather than dramatic effect

questions.explanation: A soliloquy lets an audience watch a character think and judge it at once, so it does more than deliver information. Privacy and audience taste are not the whole of the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience is asked to do during a soliloquy.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the device of speech addressed to an absent listener.

stimulus.body: The memo records a production in which an actor playing the clerk speaks to the desk clerk beside him, but the words are clearly meant for the man who left the room minutes earlier. The planner notes that the empty space on stage does the work of a listener.

questions.stem: According to the memo, the clerk's speech functions as what?

options.text: An aside that reaches an absent listener through the colleague present
An aside addressed to the colleague standing in the wings
options.misconception: locates the speech at the theatre's edge rather than onstage

options.text: A monologue delivered to the audience over the colleague's head
options.misconception: confuses addressing an absent character with direct address

options.text: A piece of stage business that passes for speech to hide an error
options.misconception: explains the speech as a mishap rather than a device

questions.explanation: The words are meant for the man who left while the colleague stands in for him, so the aside has two audiences and one missing listener. The memo reads this as deliberate.
questions.hint: Ask who is really being addressed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a difference in staging adds to a printed scene.
questions.stem: A memo compares two productions of the same scene, one where a locked door is opened slowly and one where it is thrown wide. What does the planner say the difference adds?

options.text: It adds an explanation of what happened before the scene began
options.misconception: reads staging as supplying backstory

options.text: It adds a different set of characters to the scene's conflicts
options.misconception: assumes staging changes who is present

options.text: It adds the sense that the actors have learned their lines better
options.misconception: mistakes performance quality for dramatic effect

options.text: It adds a reading of the moment that the printed dialogue leaves open

questions.explanation: Staging interprets what the dialogue leaves unspecified, so the two openings offer two readings of the same moment. Backstory and casting do not describe what staging signifies.

Because the argument introduces characters who never appear again
options.misconception: treats brevity of a scene as the sign of a subplot

options.text: Because the argument happens in a different part of the building
options.misconception: mistakes setting difference for plot function

options.text: Because the audience can watch the argument without listening closely
options.misconception: grounds the subplot in audience attention, not in function

questions.explanation: A subplot functions by pressing on the main action, and the argument over the ledger bears directly on the theft. New faces, a different room and audience attention do not make the distinction.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an early contradiction prepares a later exposure.
questions.stem: A memo asks about a scene where a character claims to have been at sea and then says a thing only a landsman would say. Why does the planner treat it as important?

answer.exemplar: The planner treats it as important because a contradiction inside a single speech plants the seed of the later exposure. The claim of experience and the detail that betrays it sit together, so the audience is given the material for the reversal months before it arrives, and the reversal then feels earned rather than sudden rather than sprung on a reader.

questions.explanation: A contradiction planted early makes a later exposure feel earned rather than sprung, which is why the memo dwells on it. The planner is describing preparation, not a lapse in writing.
questions.hint: Ask how the reversal will later be received.

options.text: It adds a rhythm and a scale of time that the page cannot fix
It adds realism, because the stage is a real room
options.misconception: treats realism as the main thing performance supplies

options.text: It adds meaning, since the play's message is clearer when spoken
options.misconception: claims staging clarifies a fixed message

questions.explanation: Performance adds what print cannot specify, above all timing and scale, and that changes how words land. Feeling, realism and clearer messaging are all things the text can already carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the page cannot fix.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Classify a scene with an uneven exchange of speech.

stimulus.body: The memo describes a scene in which one character speaks at length while the other answers only with nods and single words. The planner asks the company how such a scene should be labelled in the programme notes.

questions.stem: According to the memo, how should such a scene be labelled?

options.text: A monologue, because only one voice carries real content
options.misconception: decides the form by how much content one voice carries

options.text: A soliloquy, because the main speaker is talking to himself
options.misconception: confuses a sparse exchange with speech to an empty stage

options.text: A dialogue, because the speech is exchanged between two people
An aside, because the second character speaks only to the audience
options.misconception: misreads short replies as an aside to the audience

questions.explanation: Dialogue means speech exchanged between characters, and that is what happens however uneven the shares. One voice carrying content, an empty stage and an audience address each describe something else.
questions.hint: Ask whether speech passes between characters.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the force of a soliloquy the audience already anticipates.
questions.stem: A memo notes that a character in a soliloquy announces a decision the audience has already seen them reach privately in an earlier scene. What is the memo's concern?

options.text: That the audience will be bored hearing a decision twice
options.misconception: treats repetition as a matter of audience endurance

options.text: That the character has no right to change their mind so quickly
options.misconception: judges character consistency rather than technique

options.text: That the earlier private scene has spoiled the later declaration
options.misconception: claims a spoiler effect where the text withholds nothing

options.text: That the later speech loses force because the audience knows too much

questions.explanation: When the audience has already seen the reasoning, the character's declaration carries less dramatic weight, and that is the effect the memo names. Boredom and consistency misdescribe it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a speech made to an absent listener.
questions.stem: A memo describes a character who ends a scene by saying to the house what the absent partner would have said if he had understood. What is such a speech?

options.text: An aside, since it has an on-stage listener and the house as its second
A soliloquy, since the character is alone with the audience's attention
options.misconception: confuses an aside with a solo speech

options.text: A monologue, since no one else in the scene replies
options.misconception: decides the form by the absence of replies

options.text: A stage direction, since it reports another character's state
options.misconception: confuses a spoken line with a printed instruction

questions.explanation: An aside is speech with two audiences: the character beside him may hear part of it and the house hears the rest. It is not a soliloquy or a monologue.
questions.hint: Ask who hears what of the speech.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a printed direction about waiting has dramatic force.
questions.stem: A memo records that a stage direction asks the actor to listen for a knock that never comes, and asks why the instruction is there at all.

answer.exemplar: The instruction is there because a direction asking a character to listen builds an expectation that the house then shares, and a knock that never arrives lands precisely because the instruction created it. Nothing in the dialogue would have prepared the audience to listen for that sound, so the direction is doing the work of a whole scene's worth of expectation in four printed words.

questions.explanation: A direction asking a character to listen creates an expectation the audience shares, so the knock that never comes lands because the instruction built it. Running orders are not the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience now expects to hear.

It belongs because it lengthens the play's second half

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the detail that prepares a reversal.

stimulus.body: The memo discusses a scene in which a loyal servant is exposed as the thief. The planner asks which earlier detail, if present, would best prepare that reversal, and notes that in the play in question the servant counts the silver before leaving a room.

questions.stem: According to the memo, which detail would best prepare the reversal?

options.text: A scene in which the servant is praised by everyone present
options.misconception: thinks praise is preparation, rather than a gap in it

options.text: A habit of counting the silver before leaving a room
A line in which the servant speaks of trusting no one
options.misconception: accepts a stated attitude as a planted clue

options.text: A mention that the servant has always been honest in small matters
options.misconception: treats general character evidence as planted for reversal

questions.explanation: Preparation for a reversal plants a specific behaviour that later means the opposite of what it seemed, and the counted silver fits that pattern. Praise and general honesty do not.

options.misconception: assumes the text belongs to an earlier staging

options.text: Performance shows the words carry a meaning the text had not thought of
options.misconception: credits performance with inventing new meaning

options.misconception: invents a production cause for a textual difference

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Determine how interruptions change the form of a scene.
questions.stem: In a memo, a scene that the printed text marks as a long speech by one character is staged with the other character interrupting three times. What is the effect?

options.text: The interruptions make the speech an exchange rather than a set piece
The interruptions prove the original speech was written badly
options.misconception: reads staging as criticism of the printed writing

options.text: The interruptions show the speech is really a soliloquy in disguise
options.misconception: concludes the exchange must be one-sided in form

options.text: The interruptions turn the speech into a series of separate speeches
options.misconception: treats interruption as breaking the scene into units

questions.explanation: Interruptions make the speech an exchange, so the scene is dialogue that the printed form only suggested. Criticism of the writing, disguise as soliloquy and fragmentation each misdescribe the change.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a soliloquy reporting known information still works.
questions.stem: A memo asks whether someone who confides a fear in a soliloquy is being unusually honest, given how much the play shows them hiding.

answer.exemplar: The memo's answer is that the soliloquy is not unusual honesty but a report the audience is trusted to judge, and that its effect depends on what the plot has already made the audience feel. If the fear is something we have watched the character avoid for an hour, hearing it stated plainly is not disclosure but pressure, and the audience weighs the statement against a long record of concealment.

questions.explanation: The plot has already established the fear, so the soliloquy is a report of something the audience knows rather than a revelation of it. Expected honesty and invented listeners misdescribe the device.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience already holds.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Play text and what performance adds
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what counts as fidelity to a printed text.
questions.stem: A memo reports a reviewer who said the production was faithful to the text because every line was spoken exactly as printed.

answer.exemplar: The memo treats the reviewer's claim as too narrow, because fidelity to a text covers more than wording and a production is also a set of choices. Keeping the lines intact settles one question and leaves open the others, including how a scene is timed, where the silence falls and what a pause is made to mean, all of which the printed words leave to the company to decide.

questions.explanation: Fidelity to a text covers more than wording, since a production also makes choices about timing, space and emphasis that the printed words leave open. Keeping the lines does not settle the question.
questions.hint: Ask what else a production must decide.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's pressure on the main plot
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a thread can matter without being mentioned again.
questions.stem: A memo argues that a subplot about a broken clock in a play about a family feud is irrelevant because nobody mentions the clock in the final act.

answer.exemplar: The argument mistakes a condition of plot mechanics for the whole of dramatic function, because a thread works through what it causes rather than through whether it is named again. The clock's slow beating has set the rhythm of the household's arguments all evening, and the final act is full of characters speaking over each other, which is exactly what the clock has been predicting since the first scene.

questions.explanation: A subplot earns its place through what it causes rather than whether it is named again, and the clock can shape the family's timing and so the feud. Mention and size are the wrong tests.
questions.hint: Ask what the clock changes about the feud.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an aside from a soliloquy.
questions.stem: A memo asks what distinguishes an aside from a soliloquy in a production where the stage is divided in two.

answer.exemplar: The distinction is the second listener. An aside splits its audience between the stage and the house, so the speech is overheard by a character who can respond to part of it, while a soliloquy requires nobody onstage and is heard only by the house. Everything else, including length, verse or prose, is incidental, because both devices can be long or short and either can be written in either form.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is the second listener: an aside splits an audience between stage and house, while a soliloquy needs nobody onstage. Length and verse are not the tests.
questions.hint: Ask who else is listening.

answer.exemplar: It should be labelled as dialogue, because a refusal is an answer and the scene remains an exchange in which one side presses and the other holds. The printed form can make a long argument look like a set piece because a page shows the speech standing still, and it is only on the stage, where each refusal interrupts and redirects, that the balance of the exchange becomes visible.

questions.explanation: Refusals are answers, so the scene remains an exchange in which one side presses and the other holds back. Argumenting is not a measure of form, and nothing here addresses the house.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the demand that every reversal must be prepared.
questions.stem: A memo argues that every reversal must be prepared by planting clues, and objects to a play whose final twist rests on a chance arrival.

answer.exemplar: The objection is only half right, because preparation and chance produce different effects rather than the same effect badly achieved. A planted clue lets the audience recognise what is coming and re-read the earlier scenes, while a chance arrival produces surprise and denies the audience that second reading, so the memo can accept the twist as a legitimate effect while still rejecting it as a piece of writing.

questions.explanation: Preparation produces recognition while chance produces surprise, so the objection is only half right, and the two effects are judged differently. Chance is not preparation, and taste is not the test.
questions.hint: Ask which effect the twist depends on.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a repeated line can mean on stage that it cannot on the page.
questions.stem: The memo asks what the house hears in a staged production that repeats a line twice with exactly the same intonation.

answer.exemplar: The audience hears that the repetition is itself the meaning, since a line delivered twice with no change of tone asks the house to notice the line rather than the speaker. The printed page can show the words once and can only suggest a repeat with a dash, so the device depends on an auditorium and a body of listeners who can hear that nothing has changed at all.

questions.explanation: Repetition with no change of tone makes the repetition itself the point, which print cannot convey, since the page shows the line once. Forgetting, concealment and miscopying each miss the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the page cannot show you.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Classify a scene in which speech is passed back and forth.
questions.stem: In a memo, a character answers every question with a question, and the scene is described as a contest of speech. How is the form named?

options.text: It is a soliloquy, because the character never actually speaks
options.misconception: confuses evasiveness with speech to an empty stage

options.text: It is an aside, because the answers are meant for the house
options.misconception: invents an audience address from a rhetorical habit

options.text: It is dialogue, because the speech is passed between two characters
It is a monologue, because only one character carries the argument
options.misconception: decides the form by which character argues

questions.explanation: Questions passed back and forth are still speech exchanged, so the form is dialogue even when the content refuses to advance. Evasion and audience address do not determine the form.
questions.hint: Ask whether speech passes between characters.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the effect of a secret told to the audience.

stimulus.body: The memo describes another scene in which a customs officer tells the audience about a shipment she has agreed to let through, while a colleague in the room has just asked her, innocently, whether the cargo was all declared. The planner notes that the officer has not lied to her colleague, and that the audience knows she has.

questions.stem: According to the planner, what is the chief effect of the speech?

options.text: It lets the audience relax, since the officer has committed to the truth
options.misconception: treats the soliloquy as a relief rather than a strain

options.text: It creates the tension of an audience holding a secret the stage does not
It proves the colleague already suspects the cargo
options.misconception: reads the effect as evidence about another character

options.text: It removes the tension, since the officer has not deceived anyone onstage
options.misconception: believes honesty on stage cancels the audience's knowledge

questions.explanation: Because the audience holds what the other characters do not, every exchange plays under a strain the officer does not feel. Relief and suspicion are other readings.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience holds that the colleague does not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a speech addressed to one listener and then to the house.
questions.stem: This memo asks about a speech that one character begins to the person beside him and then continues, word for word, to the house.

options.text: It is a soliloquy, since the second half is addressed outward
options.misconception: confuses the outward half with a solo speech

options.text: It is a monologue, because one voice continues through the speech
options.misconception: decides the form by the presence of a single voice

options.text: It is a stage direction, since it tells the house what to do
options.misconception: confuses spoken words with a written instruction

options.text: It is an aside in two stages, holding both audiences at once

questions.explanation: A speech that begins for one listener and continues word for word to the house holds both audiences at once, which is an aside in two stages. Soliloquy and monologue are the wrong labels.
questions.hint: Ask who is being held at once.
